title: Why the United States and Iran Keep Fighting While They Negotiate
gist: CSIS argues the U.S.-Iran pattern of striking while negotiating — 'talk-fight' — is not a breakdown of diplomacy but the most effective negotiating mode for both sides and paradoxically the fastest route to peace. The contrarian core: escalation risk in talk-fight is 'vastly overstated' because incentives to contain fighting coexist with incentives to fight, whereas a ceasefire-first process would hand power to spoilers and be structurally fragile.

insights.claim: For both the United States and Iran, fighting while simultaneously negotiating — 'talk-fight' — is the most effective way to advance their interests and paradoxically also the fastest path to peace, so commentators who declare negotiations dead after every exchange of fire are wrong.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Do not treat individual strikes as evidence that diplomacy has collapsed — the strike cadence is part of the negotiation, which argues for fading violence-driven risk spikes.
insights.quote: Every time one side shoots, commentators declare negotiations dead. They are wrong.
insights.locator: Iran and the United States are cycling through moments of fighting and calm

insights.claim: Applying Clausewitz's framework, Iranian attacks on tankers, U.S. strikes on Iranian port facilities, and Iranian missiles fired at Gulf neighbors such as Kuwait and Qatar are political communication rather than an interruption of talks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Gives an interpretive filter for reading strike headlines: violence signals bargaining position, so read it for concessions demanded, not for war expansion.
insights.quote: They are not halting negotiations but continuing them.
insights.locator: The grandfather of grand strategy, Carl von Clausewitz

insights.claim: In talk-fight, U.S. violence signals resolve and overwhelming military might to force Iranian concessions, while Iranian violence reminds the world it can shut the Strait of Hormuz any time it chooses and that time is on its side.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Iranian strikes are leverage demonstrations over Hormuz, meaning shipping-disruption signaling continues right up to a deal rather than tapering before it.
insights.locator: Iran and the United States have defaulted to talk-fight

insights.claim: The traditional ceasefire-first approach is slow and structurally fragile because months get consumed by preconditions and negotiating about negotiations — parties in the Vietnam War spent 10 weeks arguing over the shape of the table for the Paris talks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Anyone waiting for a ceasefire as the precondition for de-risking should expect a multi-month process that can reset at the first shot.
insights.quote: the parties in the Vietnam War spent 10 weeks arguing over the shape of the table for the Paris talks
insights.locator: Talk-fight is a counterintuitive way to negotiate

insights.claim: In many conflicts neither side has incentive for a ceasefire: the side with battlefield momentum does not want to squander it, and the losing side keeps fighting to reach an elusive and usually undefinable 'position of strength' from which to negotiate.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explains why ceasefire headlines repeatedly fail to materialize — the structural incentive is absent, so price ceasefire optimism cheaply.
insights.locator: In many cases, both sides have little incentive for a ceasefire

insights.claim: If a ceasefire does arrive, spoilers suddenly hold all the power: a rogue actor, third-party intervention, or a miscommunication or mistake can restart fighting, because negotiations built on a wobbly base of barely contained violence invite disruption.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A signed ceasefire would raise, not lower, headline fragility — an argument against treating a ceasefire announcement as a durable de-risking event.
insights.quote: If you build negotiations on a wobbly base of barely contained violence, you are asking for disruption and trouble.

insights.claim: Iran is an exceptionally difficult negotiating partner with the patience to outwait its counterparts, the domestic power to ignore the suffering of its people, and a track record of winning negotiations.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Implies a long timeline and unfavourable U.S. terms — bias duration expectations for the conflict toward the longer end.
insights.quote: It has the patience to outwait its counterparts, the domestic power to ignore the suffering of its people, and a track record of winning negotiations.
insights.locator: Further, Iran has a reputation for being an exceptionally difficult negotiating partner

insights.claim: Iran cares little if the global economy suffers because a decades-long comprehensive sanctions regime has already largely cut it off from the global financial system, and for the regime at least a perception that it won is essential to survival.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Economic-pain pressure has limited traction on Iran, so global-market damage is not a self-limiting brake on the conflict.
insights.quote: Iran is largely cut off from the global financial system anyway
insights.locator: For the Iranian regime, at least a perception that it won

insights.claim: Iran could outwait the United States and is eager to see it sink money and munitions into the conflict, an outcome its friends in Moscow and Beijing are also happy to see.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Russian and Chinese interest in a prolonged U.S. drain reduces the odds of external pressure toward resolution.
insights.quote: Their friends in Moscow and Beijing are happy to see it, too.
insights.locator: Iran could very well outwait the United States

themes.theme: Risks, tails, and the escalation contrarian call

insights.claim: The global economy is suffering paroxysms of uncertainty from every wave of violence in the U.S.-Iran conflict, even though the casualty count is relatively low.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Market volatility is tied to strike cadence rather than to casualty scale — a recurring, tradeable volatility pattern.
insights.quote: the global economy is suffering paroxysms of uncertainty from every wave of violence
insights.locator: Still, there are risks to this approach

insights.claim: The main tail risk is that Tehran overestimates Washington's patience and provokes a bruising U.S. response against military-adjacent targets affecting the local population — bridges and oil-related targets including Kharg Island — which could imperil Iranian economic recovery for years.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Kharg Island is the named escalation tripwire; a strike there would remove Iranian export capacity durably and is the specific tail to hedge.
insights.locator: For the parties, Tehran could overestimate Washington’s patience

insights.claim: The widely cited risk that fighting escalates is usually vastly overstated: escalation is less likely in a talk-fight scenario than when fighting was intense with no negotiations ongoing, because incentives to contain the fighting exist alongside incentives to fight.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The central against-consensus call: sell escalation fear during active negotiations rather than buying it on each strike headline.
insights.quote: This possibility is usually vastly overstated.

insights.claim: The prescription is that negotiations should continue with stubborn resolve to be immune to disruption, because both parties will claw for advantage away from the table and both believe violence is a legitimate tool — talking on regardless is the fastest route to real peace and relative economic normalcy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A negotiation process explicitly designed to survive strikes is the leading indicator of eventual resolution — watch for talks continuing through attacks, not pausing.
insights.quote: The fastest way to achieve a real peace for the people of the Gulf and relative economic normalcy for the world is to talk on, no matter what.
insights.locator: Negotiations should continue with a stubborn resolve
